one_liner: Pure-Rust rebuild of mimalloc's design; slightly fewer instructions than mimalloc, jemalloc and glibc malloc under callgrind.
what_it_does: A general-purpose allocator that reimplements mimalloc v2.4.5's segment/page architecture in Rust, usable as a Rust #[global_allocator] (rusty_alloc-api crate), as a mi_*-compatible C ABI (rusty_alloc_ffi) or as an LD_PRELOAD malloc/free interposer (rusty_alloc_override cdylib). The same codebase also targets wasm32-unknown-unknown (via memory.grow) and no_std bare metal such as ESP32-S3, where it competes with dlmalloc and esp-alloc.
how_it_is_fast: mimalloc's free-list sharding: 32 MiB segments sliced into 64 KiB spans, per-page local free lists, and a four-state lock-free cross-thread free protocol (loom-verified). The authors tuned the hot paths instruction by instruction: free is 21 instructions vs mimalloc's 25 (pointer-to-page resolve through a per-slice owner table in the segment header), all divisions were replaced by shifts and a reciprocal table, and the Rust GlobalAlloc methods are #[inline] so rustc's __rust_alloc shims carry the fast path.
when_to_use: Pure-Rust projects that want a mimalloc-class allocator without a C toolchain in the build (no cc/cmake dependency).
Shipping one allocator across Linux, macOS, Windows, wasm32 and an ESP32-class MCU from a single dependency.
wasm modules with churny allocation (many live blocks of 8-512 B), where the README measures 4.9-7.3x over dlmalloc for +2,435 bytes gzipped.
ESP32-S3 firmware with RAM to spare where small-object allocation throughput matters (1.44-3.94x faster than esp-alloc 0.11 per alloc/free pair).
When you want double frees to abort rather than silently corrupt (mimalloc release builds accept them), with an opt-in encrypted free-list 'secure' mode.
when_not_to_use: If you need wall-clock evidence: every x86 claim is a callgrind instruction count; the workspace manifest says wall-clock measurement still needs a quiet machine, and whole-program gains over mimalloc are 0-4%.

Memory-constrained MCUs: needs a 64 KiB RAM floor vs 8 KiB for esp-alloc, held 21 size classes at once vs 24, returned 357 NULLs in 50,000 hostile churn allocations vs 0, and refuses 64 KiB-aligned requests; the README itself says esp-alloc wins memory footprint by 8.5x.
wasm code dominated by large (2 KB) tight alloc/free loops, where it runs 0.55-0.83x as fast as dlmalloc.
Long-running processes that must give memory back by default: freed memory stays committed (purge_delay -1); one consumer saw 461 MB retained where the Windows heap dropped to 4 MB.

Risk-averse production use: the repository dates from 2026, has 3 stars, an open blockmap race issue (#8), and a closed issue (#37) titled 'Whatever you are trying to achieve here, please stop!'; adoption figures in the README are first-party and inconsistent.

integration.dependencies: none required beyond libc on Unix and windows-sys on Windows; optional portable-atomic for targets without native atomics
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88 (rust-version), edition 2024; repo pins 1.97.1 for development
integration.platforms: x86-64 and aarch64 on Linux, macOS and Windows; wasm32-unknown-unknown; no_std ESP32-S3 (Xtensa); RISC-V bare-metal targets listed but the toolchain file says the crate does not yet build for them
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe by default (per-thread heaps, lock-free cross-thread free, abandonment and adoption); bare-metal builds must set --cfg ra_single_threaded
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — LD_PRELOAD interposer and mi_* C ABI for C/C++ programs, #[global_allocator] for Rust; not a link-time replacement for libmimalloc's full option/stat surface

gotchas: Bare-metal builds need three settings: --cfg ra_single_threaded, --cfg ra_small_profile, and a Region<N> handed over once; without ra_small_profile it builds and links but every allocation returns null (SEGMENT_SIZE stays 32 MiB).
Size the embedded region with good_region_size()/region_for(), not a round number or a plain static [u8; N], or segments are stranded or the region is refused (FERR_MISALIGNED).

The lua callgrind numbers move about 0.26% run to run (hash seed not pinnable); only perl and sqlite counts are bit-repeatable, and the allocator-only ratio is attributed by object, so the glibc arm has no allocator-only figure.
alloc::stats() counters only exist in debug builds; the opt-in blockmap feature has an open race report under abandon/adopt at low core counts (issue #8).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Talc or rlsf when you want one mimalloc-style allocator spanning servers, wasm and an ESP32 rather than a wasm/embedded-only TLSF or arena design; on servers the C and C++ siblings (v8malloc, FastAlloc, Spaces) and upstream mimalloc itself have more mileage and wall-clock data.
verified_claims_summary: Under callgrind with LD_PRELOAD on x86-64 Linux (CPU model and compiler flags not stated), short lua, perl and sqlite one-liner workloads ran 0.96 / 0.99 / 1.00 of mimalloc v2.4.5's whole-program instructions (0.84-0.98 of jemalloc, 0.81-0.99 of glibc malloc), with the allocator's own instructions at 0.52 / 0.81 / 0.83 of mimalloc's. Wall-clock numbers exist only for wasm32 in node (churn 4.9-7.3x vs dlmalloc, 2 KB loop 0.55-0.83x) and a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 at 240 MHz (1.44-3.94x vs esp-alloc 0.11).
status_note: Very active (multiple releases since September 2026, now 2.2.x, semver-checked API) and MIT-licensed, but young, single-organisation and marketed heavily; bench scripts (bench/icount-arms.sh, oracle/build.sh) make the instruction counts reproducible on your own machine.
